text: Edward A. "Ted" Irving, CM FRSC FRS (27 May 1927 – 25 February 2014), was a British-Canadian geologist who worked with the Geological Survey of Canada. His research on paleomagnetism provided the first physical evidence supporting the theory of continental drift. Irving was born on 25 May 1925 and raised in Colne, in the Pennine Hills of east Lancashire, England. In 1945, he was conscripted into the British Army and served in the Middle East infantry. In 1948, he began studying geology at the University of Cambridge, earning a Bachelor of Arts degree in 1951. He then spent a year as a research assistant with Keith Runcorn in the geology and geophysics department before entering graduate studies. At the time, the history of Earth's magnetic field was known only for the past few centuries due to magnetic observatories. With fellow students Kenneth Creer and Jan Hospers, Irving used a magnetometer, recently designed by Patrick Blackett, to analyze magnetic directions in rocks. He discovered significant discrepancies between the current magnetic field direction and those recorded in Precambrian rocks in Scotland’s highlands, concluding that Scotland had shifted relative to the geomagnetic pole. He also determined that India had moved northward by 6000 km and rotated by more than 30°, confirming Alfred Wegener’s 1912 predictions of continental drift. In 1954, Irving attempted to obtain a PhD, but his examiners, unfamiliar with the emerging field, refused to grant him the degree. Despite this, he secured a research fellow position at the Australian National University in Canberra. Over the next ten years, he studied Australia’s ancient latitudes and published around 30 papers, demonstrating the continent’s southward movement since the Permian period. In 1965, he submitted papers to Cambridge and was awarded a ScD, the highest degree available at the time. Irving met his wife Sheila, a Canadian citizen, in Australia, and in 1964 they moved to Ottawa, Ontario, where he began working as a research officer for the Dominion Observatory with the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. In 1966, he returned to England to teach geophysics at the University of Leeds, then returned to Ottawa in 1967 as a research scientist in the Earth Physics Branch of the Department of Energy, Mines, and Resources. In 1981, he moved to Sidney, British Columbia, to establish a paleomagnetism laboratory at the Pacific Geoscience Centre with the Earth Physics Branch, which later became part of the Geological Survey of Canada. There, he mapped the lateral movements and rotations of Vancouver Island and other parts of the Cordillera relative to the Precambrian Canadian Shield. In 2005, Irving was semi-retired, investigating the geomagnetic field in the Precambrian to understand crustal deformation and latitude changes. He and Sheila had four children. Irving died during the night of 24 February 2014 in Saanich, British Columbia. He published a total of 205 papers, including the first book on paleomagnetism. He received the Gondwanaland Gold Medal from the Mining, Geological, and Metallurgical Society of India, the Logan Medal from the Geological Association of Canada (1975), the Walter H. Bucher Medal from the American Geophysical Union (1979), the J. Tuzo Wilson Medal from the Canadian Geophysical Union (1984), the Arthur L. Day Medal from the Geological Society of America (1997), and the Wollaston Medal from the Geological Society of London (2005). He was made a fellow of the Royal Society of Canada (FRSC) in 1973 and of the Royal Society of London (FRS) in 1979. In 1998, he was elected to the National Academy of Sciences, and in 2003 he was invited to be a Member of the Order of Canada. He also received an honorary degree from the University of Victoria in 1999.
